segmentRevenue.title: Segment revenue: Consumer vs tesa
segmentRevenue.content:
Beiersdorf runs two independent segments: Consumer (NIVEA, Eucerin/Derma, La Prairie, Chantecaille, Health Care brands -- about 83% of group sales) and tesa (industrial and consumer adhesive tapes, about 17%).

For Beiersdorf: tesa is smaller but structurally higher-margin and less brand-dependent than Consumer; it has historically grown steadily even while Consumer's NIVEA-driven growth has slowed, though it is itself exposed to the European auto and consumer-electronics cycle.

What to watch:

  • Whether tesa's EBIT margin (~16%) continues to outrun Consumer's
  • Whether tesa can offset Consumer softness, or is itself cyclical at the same time (as in H1 2026)

organicGrowth.title: Organic growth by segment and brand
organicGrowth.content:
Organic growth strips out currency and portfolio (M&A/disposal) effects, leaving volume and price/mix -- the number management and analysts use to judge underlying momentum, shown here for the two segments and the three brands/brand groups Beiersdorf breaks out separately: Derma (Eucerin/Aquaphor), La Prairie and Health Care.

For Beiersdorf: NIVEA (~43% of group sales, the largest single piece of Consumer but not broken out as its own column here) turned negative in H1 2026 (-6.8%) after a weak FY2025, dragging Consumer growth down even as Derma kept growing double digits. La Prairie swung from three years of decline (2023-2025, as deep as -14.9% in one quarter) to tentative positive quarters in late 2025/2026 on China e-commerce and new leadership -- the single most volatile line on this chart.

What to watch:

  • Whether La Prairie's recovery holds for consecutive quarters or reverses, since it is concentrated in Chinese consumer sentiment and global travel retail
  • NIVEA's 'Rebalancing' turnaround, which management does not expect to show results before 2027
  • Whether Derma's double-digit growth is large enough yet to offset a declining NIVEA within Consumer

segmentEbit.title: Adjusted segment EBIT: Consumer vs tesa
segmentEbit.content:
Adjusted segment EBIT is each segment's operating profit before special/one-off items -- the profitability counterpart to the revenue split above.

For Beiersdorf: only FY2024 and FY2025 are disclosed on this basis, so the chart cannot yet show a trend; group EBIT margin excluding special factors already fell from 16.1% to 15.5% in H1 2026 as negative FX, cost inflation and incremental NIVEA marketing spend outpaced pricing, with both segments' margins down year-on-year.

What to watch:

  • Whether tesa's margin keeps exceeding Consumer's as the smaller, more industrial segment
  • Consumer margin trend through the NIVEA turnaround, which adds ~EUR100m of marketing spend before any offsetting growth is expected

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Beiersdorf AG: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Beiersdorf AG: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Beiersdorf AG: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Beiersdorf AG: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Beiersdorf AG: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Beiersdorf AG: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Beiersdorf AG: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Beiersdorf AG: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Beiersdorf AG: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Beiersdorf AG: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
